item.title: Itch Anniversary
item.description: Yesterday was exactly one year since I requested a payout of the money accrued at Itch.io. Of course this did not go as planned, and no payment was forthcoming. I had it down on my calendar to review the situation, and when the reminder popped up, my heart sank. I should try again to get paid out, but I didn’t want to, was the effort worth the few dollars it may or may not earn me? I had already sent four support messages, why wouldn’t a fifth go unanswered too. Ultimately I decided to post to Itch’s reddit forum. Within 6 hours the payment was made! You can make you own assessment of what motivated Itch to act.

item.title: AI Coding Week X
item.description:
Not sure how long I’ve been trying out AI-assisted coding. There was the first 4 weeks (weeks 1, 2, 3), followed by a long gap, and then I started again. Probably its has been a total of 10 weeks by now, but I’m not sure. Let’s just call it week X. It seems like a good time to reflect again, as another project has just finished and its worth noting what I have learned. Short version is that I’m still impressed, but a little less so than before as some of its fiddly realities become clearer.

When I renewed my subscription to Claude Pro, I decided to get things going by finishing an old unfinished project. A few years ago I started a Scala version of the Ink interpreter (a language to write stories in games). After implementing about half of the tutorial, it started getting much harder and I abandoned the side-project. Based on my first go at AI coding, I thought it could get it finished in maybe two weeks, then I would move on. It took over 6 weeks.

At first I thought it was me. Had the month I had been doing other things made me forget and overestimate Claude’s ability? My weekly usage was evaporating so quickly. Once I asked it to debug an issue and it went around in circles burning through my entire 5-hour usage allowance in 20 minutes without a fix. I was so angry I almost ragequit and considered asking for a refund. But I didn’t. Instead I went online and found many people with the same problems. It definitely seems like Anthropic had changed something and made it much less useful and/or more expensive. Indeed a week later the company announced that there were bugs in the system, that they had now fixed. The system has gotten somewhat better since then; returning to usefulness. I would say it feels about as “intelligent” as those first promising weeks, but it definitely seems like my usage allowance is less. Now, it can do the tasks I give it, but my 5-hour allowance is always gone in well under an hour of usage. It also seems highly variable, some days lots get done, others very little.

Reading other people’s similar experiences, two things become clear. Firstly, Anthropic is constantly tinkering with their system. These changes do not seem particularly well directed or communicated. I feel like I’m blind testing the system for them and paying for the privilege (not a great customer experience). Secondly, all of AI-assisted coding acts like a cargo cult. There is lots of advice on how to make the most of these AIs and its often contradictory or not relevant or just doesn’t work or outdated (or soon to be outdated by another tweak!). All advice seems to be anecdotal. Much of it seems to be based on asking the AIs what they think (hmmm).

Despite the above, here are some of my anecdotal observations on AI coding assistants:

  • They are fast and on a good day can produce in under a hour something that would take me a multiple of that.
  • On small (10 min or so) constrained tasks they perform very well. If I give them a broken test that exercises a bug and ask them to fix it, then 90% of the time it is done quickly and efficiently.
  • Mechanical refactors are a waste of usage. They will do them, but slower than me and cost a large amount of usage in the process.
  • NEVER ask them to do more than 1 thing at a time (eg. fix these three bugs) they will get lost.
  • The larger the task, the more corners they will cut and the more careful you need to be!
  • They need to be constantly reminded to create tests and to not change existing (correct) tests. Once in order to “fix” a bug, Claude just changed the test to something completely wrong. Now I have multiple layers of instructions to never do that.
  • They write like a junior dev being paid by the number of lines produced. So much code, much of it unnecessary.
  • They are very bad learners! An example, Claude creates a plan for a new feature, but it doesn’t seem right to me. I ask about it and Claude says there is a better way, “make errors uncompilable”, as in its user-specified (by me) instructions. If it knew that was in its instructions, why did it not use it the first time? So I get it to do it again and it’s better. On a similar task the very next day, it forgets and does the same thing again. I question it, and it goes, yes of course “make errors uncompilable”!
  • Telling them to remember does not work. They need to be constantly reminded. Now my prompts often include a bunch of useful tips or coding philosophies so they always have them readily to hand.
  • If I’m not careful, they can easily create more code than I can usefully review or understand. This has already happened a few times in this project.
  • They are excellent at creating/updating notes, task lists, designs and other documentation. In general, they are good organisers.

That last point is one of the main reasons I will continue using AIs. Recently in my work I was awful at remembering why something was done or what tasks remained. I think I was better when younger and working professionally on the same project every day. Now I’m older and some time can pass between coding sessions so things get lost (and/or my memory is worse). Knowing the task list and reasoning is always there actually helps motivate me to work more regularly. Definitely a huge benefit as just turning up and moving slightly forward every week makes it easier to keep going as a habit (something I lost in recent years). I’ve also come to a good accommodation with the usage allowances. I do 3-4 hours work a day with regular breaks (across the 5-hour usage window) for 4-5 days/week (stopping when the weekly usage is exhausted). So normally I have Monday/Tuesday off, useful for completing other tasks (like writing this post).

What’s next? Time to try a larger project, something hopefully more useful. It it works out, then it will be its own topic. Thus this will be the last of these AI Coding posts for the foreseeable future.

item.title: Westworld
item.description:
I recently decided to finish watching Westworld. I watched the first couple of season when they were the released, and my opinions seemed to match public perception: the first season was excellent; the second was a great disappointment and a slide towards mediocrity. It has been some time since the last two seasons were released, but I understand that the general opinion is that they did not reverse the descent.

Well I liked season 3 (however, season 4 was not good). I think it opened up the setting in an interesting manner. The story was not as good as season 1, but we got a better understanding of how the wider world outside the park worked. It was an ambitious attempt to show something new within a familiar Westworld story, and it mostly delivered. It felt like a modern cyberpunk (as opposed to the 80’s nostalgia of most recent cyberpunk).

In an ahistorical story (like all fantasy and most sci-fi), the wider environment usually seems to exist solely for the purpose of moving the story forward. I do not normally get a sense that these are worlds that exist outside of that particular movie or TV show (books tend to be better). It is a notable achievement when there is a show that does feel like it has a complete world (that existed before the start and will continue after the end of the story being told). Game of Thrones and The Expanse are recent examples.

Westworld season 1 was not a show like this, the setting was very much built for the purposes of the story, literally! So respect to the writers for the difficult and thankless task (most people will not care, and that is fine) of retrofitting a fuller, more interesting world onto the show. I appreciate the inclination to try something difficult, even if it doesn’t completely succeed. For a similar reason I have a better opinion of the second Matrix movie than most people (sooo much exposition, but at least for a good cause).

item.title: New Zealand
item.description:
Earlier this month I spent a fortnight in New Zealand, and now I’m over the inevitable post-travel illness. The trip was split into two parts: a week in Auckland with a side trip to Rotorua; followed by a week in Queenstown and its surrounds. I wouldn’t recommend this itinerary. Not because it was bad trip, quite the opposite. It was not long enough in either location. Best would be to hire a campervan (we just had a hire car for a few days) and make a 3+ week road trip from Auckland to Queenstown. The country is very pretty and easy to to travel (for an Australian at least).

Auckland seems like a pleasant, liveable city. Less spread out than Perth (smaller population too, despite being the largest city in NZ) with more happening (judging by the posters). It even has a nice nearby island, Waiheke, with beaches and wineries. There was activity in the CBD and many decent multicultural food options. We had some very good West Chinese noodles. Some of this may be because there are a great number of tourists. We were told 7% of the NZ economy is tourism!

Tourism is very apparent on reaching Queenstown. The place seems built for sightseeing. And such sights! This is a beautiful part of the world, no surprise it is often used in films. I had heard that the NZ economy was not doing so well. However, Queenstown and surrounding towns seem to be thriving. Lots of building, lots of people, lots to do. Interestingly we met nearly no locals. The people serving tourists in hotels, restaurants and on tours were all recent arrivals. On our tour to Milford Sound, the guide told us he had been in the country only a year, and walked into that job right after arrival.

Some photos from the trip are in a short slideshow available here.

item.title: Old Films
item.description:
Some thoughts…

I recently watched Last Year at Marienbad (part of the 60’s French New Wave) on Kanopy (a great streaming service if you have a library card). I enjoyed the film despite it being slow and without much of a plot (a man tries to convince a women that they know each other for 90 minutes). There was some clever film making and the more subtle cuts worked well to disorient the viewer (or at least me). This movie is considered a classic. I’ve heard about it many times over the decades. Would it still be if released for the first time today? I doubt it, despite thinking it’s a good movie. It is too similar to many arthouse or experimental films I’ve seen.

The French New Wave were known for breaking accepted movie conventions. Now their rule-breaking is part of the conventions. Last Year at Marienbad reminded me a little of Before Sunrise. Parts from Spike Lee or Tarantino movies remind me of another French New Wave film, Breathless. I wish people wouldn’t copy the style of introspective dream sequences from 8½ (because I think they rarely succeed). Its not only the more arty filmmakers. The excellent over-the-top action of Hardboiled spawned a wave of inferior over-the-top 90’s action movies. More successfully, the gritty survival-action of The Raid inspired great action in modern movies (like John Wick).

Years ago I saw Citizen Kane because it was acclaimed as a classic. I wasn’t impressed. It didn’t make much of an impact. I guessed the ending and it didn’t seem that special. Later I learnt how films were different prior to Citizen Kane and what did actually made it special and groundbreaking. Films now are made by people influenced by people influenced by people influenced by Citizen Kane. The lessons have infused into the background knowledge of people both making and watching films, without them ever having necessarily seen the origin.

The best example of this is Psycho. Not the 1960 original that broke new ground and shocked (and yes, I’ve seen Peeping Tom, but they were made concurrently on different continents, so how much could they effect each other?). Instead the 1998 Gus Van Sant remake. The two are almost exactly the same shot-for-shot and word-for-word. So if the first is a classic, the same movie nearly 40 years later must also be good? Nope, the reviews for the remake are awful, it bombed at the box office, and is now largely forgotten. What is the difference? It can’t be entirely the audience’s changing tastes. Critics often praised the original while condemning the remake. Is it the original was first and was original; the remake just a well made copy?

In gamedev there is a saying that ideas are worthless, execution is everything (I’ve heard similar among tech startups). Watch Last Year at Marienbad reminded me that sometimes an original idea is worth something too.

item.title: AI Coding Week 3
item.description:
Week 3 of Claude Code test is complete (week 1 here and week 2 here). It is unlikely I’ll write a week 4 report. Not because I am unhappy, but the opposite. I think this experiment has shown that there is some value in the current coding assistants for me. Thus the next task is to think about how I can use them productively (given their advantages and flaws), which is probably more than a one week job.

Speaking of flaws the week started with a stark reminder. I tried out Claude Code on the Web, it did not go well. The idea is to provide an isolated environment accessible anywhere so that you can set Claude loose without concern. However, I quickly found a concern! While setting up my current Scala project I discovered the environment did not have the sbt build tool installed. This is completely normal, and I have installed it many times, it is a simple process. I asked Claude to install it (as I couldn’t find a way to get terminal access for myself) and walked away to do something else. After 10 or so minutes it had burned through 9% of my weekly quota failing to install sbt!

When Claude has a problem it keeps trying things. It doesn’t stop and reassess the instruction. In this case it is likely it was just not possible; that the environment was too locked down. Claude didn’t care. I was unimpressed because this is Claude’s own environment, but apparently it doesn’t know its own limitations in its own environment. Also, it doesn’t seem to be aware of its own quota/usage (I asked if it could be, and it replied no). So just just burns through it.

After calming down for a day, I got back to testing. Claude was tasked to create a Godot based prototype client for the little game previously created. Behold…

About as good as I could do, but much faster. If I wanted to sell copies of the game, it would need to be massively improved with a prettier interface. That would realistically require a great deal of time, testing and iteration if I did it, or (like with my last game) paying someone with better UI design sense to do it. Although. for just getting started with development and testing work, this is fine. So a success.

As that task barely cost a third of my weekly quota, I then assigned it to create a website to import the datafiles of various fitness apps that I use and combine the results into a single view. It did it so well I suspect this is similar to Claude’s standard training jobs. Then with the little remaining quota I questioned Claude about the best way to structure projects to keep its usage low. Its responses matched my anecdotal experiences over the last few weeks.

So the experiment is over. Not sure what I will do with Claude next week, perhaps some little long abandoned toy side-projects. If I decide to pay for it in future, I will need to have a plan with long term goals. It can be very easy to just treat this as a fun game, but if that’s all I use it for, real games would be better (and cheaper). If nothing else it has forced me to think about how I develop software (in order to effectively instruct Claude) and what I should be doing with my time.

item.title: Itch Games
item.description:
Given my annoyance at Itch.io (they still have not paid me!) I thought it time to work through my backlog of games there, so I can abandon my account. No links to Itch (is PageRank still active?).

Astrologaster (4 hrs) - A well-made story game of an astrologer trying to become a doctor in 16th century London. Based partially on real people/events! The story seems linear, and a little too long. By the end I was just choosing diagnoses at random. It didn’t seem to make much difference, the story continued the way it wanted. I liked the humour and historicity (I looked a few people/events up on Wikipedia). Mildly interesting game elevated by surprisingly good production values.

A Mortician’s Tale (1 hr) - Very short (I finished in an hour) story game about what happens to our bodies after death. Partly epistolary, part point and click, the story is very linear, but that doesn’t matter as it’s finished quickly (the secret to good story games in my opinion). A good game that meets its ambitions.

Flash Point (1 hr) - Computer adaptation of the cooperative boardgame of putting out fires and rescuing people. It felt clumsy, repetitive and random. I just couldn’t get into it.

From Orbit (2hrs) - A roguelike RTS, that sees your spaceship trying to escape from “something” (not clear what) by travelling through a series of planets. On each planet you have to battle waves of enemies while collecting resources. Over time you can power up your crew and gain new crew members. At least I think that is the game - there is no tutorial or instructions so I just had to work it out as I went. A bit clunky and repetitive, this feels more like a decent beginning of the game development process rather than a finished product.

Attrition: Tactical Fronts (2hrs) - I feel for the developers of this fast turn-based tactics game set in WW1. It reminds me of my game in that there is something here, but the game just doesn’t quite get there. It seems to be online multiplayer focussed, but since it is 7 years old, no one is around to play. I went through just over 2/3rds of the solo campaign and faced no significant challenge, winning all easily - largely due to the AI making regular game ending mistakes. Entertaining for a short time.

Death and Taxes (4hrs) - I loved the idea of this point-and-click story game where you play as a Grim Reaper (apparently there are many of them) choosing who should die in a bureaucratic office run by Fate. It also works well in practice too. At first I wasn’t sure what I was supposed to be doing, but soon discovered that is part of the game. I played through once, enjoyed it, and don’t plan to do so again despite some replayability built in. Very good.

The Stillness of the Wind (1hr) - A farming simulator where an old woman tends a farm alone, while receiving increasingly worrisome letters from her departed family. Not really my sort of game, and I found the controls clunky.

item.title: AI Coding Week 2
item.description:
Week Two of testing out Claude code is complete (see week 1 here). Actually, the week ended on Wednesday when my weekly quota ended. That is despite not using it on Saturday at all, and only a little on Sunday. The 7 quota seems to be more like a 3 day quota. I wonder if that is a sales technique?

This (half) week I tried out creating a greenfield project. A simple non-graphical web game that has little commercial prospects, so I don’t care how it goes. Claude just finished a prototype in its allotted time, shaking out a few issues - a worthwhile result.

First I asked it to help out with designing the system. I gave it a couple of paragraphs describing the game and some technical constraints. It then asked long series of very good questions before outputting some design docs and an implementation plan. It mostly understood the brief, and the plan was decent. I was very impressed with this stage, I would happily use Claude again help the design and planning phase of development. The main benefit is that I had Claude log all its decisions and work. Now I have a complete list of ideas, alternatives and the reasons decisions were made - something I’m usually too lazy to bother with (and then regret later).

Then I had Claude work step-by-step (24 steps in the plan) in development. It ran out of quota on the last step (online deployment), but I can run it locally so its not too bad. I looked a little at the code produced, but apart from code duplication and superfluous config, it looked ok. So I mostly let it do its own thing. Often it would find its own mistakes, eventually.

The end result is… decent. Very simple gameplay and a frontend that is “backend developer” quality (so the same as me). It is largely what I asked it to do. I haven’t found any bugs, but do have a long list of improvements and ideas. Thus, I would declare it a successful prototype. Claude produced more than I could have done in 3 days for sure, and probably more than I could do in a solid week’s work. Although there are a few things I would have improved along the way, so I like to think my quality would be higher.

There are two big issues I see:

  • Quota limits: At first I thought this week it was getting more done considering the quota used. However, it just seems to be small projects (such as the initial greenfield work) result in a smaller context, and thus lower quota usage. I’m not sure what the solution is. Maybe break projects into smaller components. Maybe avoid long running sessions (don’t do more than a couple of compactions). Some experimentation is required.
  • It also makes me want to let it free reign - or as Claude calls it, YOLO mode! Although I’m way to scared and careful with my data to allow it. I’ll try looking at isolated environments like Claude Code Web or Sprites.io to see if they work well enough.

Next week I’ll try getting Claude to create something in Godot (maybe a client for this week’s game). If it can do that then I can see this being useful, despite the limitations.

item.title: AI Coding Week 1
item.description:
In the last couple of months I have been hearing increasingly positive reviews on LLM coding assistants. I gave the LLM’s a quick try almost a year ago (for free) and was not particularly impressed. However, the buzz now is they have massively improved and that the business of coding has changed. Being curious, I signed up for a month of Claude Code Pro to see if this view has any merit. I’ll aim to write up my thoughts at the end of each week - this is week 1.

I should begin by saying this post is not written by LLM in any way. Nor are any of the posts in this blog (so far at least).

Before starting I read many posts with advice about how to get the most of AI assistants (for examples, see here, here and here). They often talk about the benefits of planning and constraining LLMs with testing harnesses and linting tools to guide its work. Thus I decided to start by reviewing an existing Scala project containing a library of code useful in many of my game projects. It had >75% test coverage and linters already setup, plus a compiler option set to break the build on warnings (not just errors). So I set Claude to work reviewing the code, fixing bugs and suggesting improvements.

My impression was “damn, this really works.” It has fixed around 30 issues or improvements it found in the code. Most were minor, but a couple were embarrassing bugs. There were also 2 false positives - things it said were bugs initially, but on further investigation (by Claude) turned out not to be bugs. I also set it to improve test coverage, and it did so sensibly to over 85%. I reviewed closely every line added, removed or updated. Most of the fixes were small and were committed unchanged, a couple of the larger ones needed some changes to better match my (functional) style.

Overall, based on my experience in the industry, Claude acted like a good and attentive junior developer. It went through and diligently found bugs, long after my eyes would have glazed over. I had a comment “// TODO: nasty hack” and it found a 1 line fix (replacing my 3 lines) in a part of the Standard Scala library I didn’t know about - that impressed me. At first it would miss some things, or have trouble working out parts of the project (like the coverage system). However, after updating its config it worked much better. The main reason I describe it as junior is because it largely offered no pushback or initiative. It always agreed with me and told me I was right (unlikely :). It did exactly what I asked and only that. Probably this is by design, and maybe because it was working in an existing project. It also had a tendency to produce procedural code, which doesn’t fit a functional language like Scala. Still it definitely provided value and at a cost orders of magnitude below an actual junior dev.

Still for a small independent dev like me, cost is the main issue with Claude. Or at least, the amount of usage for the cost. Claude gives a 5-hour and 7 day quota. I regularly hit my 5-hour quota after a hour, and always before the 2 hour mark. My 7-day quota was reached over a day before the deadline. This is despite trying a few tricks to keep the usage low, like downgrading the effort in config. I also add a status line giving continuous notice of usage and what the cost would be if I allowed Claude to exceed its quota. I’m very happy going over quota is off by default - the non-plan costs rise fast and quickly exceed any reasonable budget I would allow. I will have to watch this closely, otherwise it will severely restrict what is possible.

Overall I am impressed. It’s not perfect, but definitely useful. It has made me think about my design philosophy, rather than being completely focussed on implementation details. Next week, when my quota resets, I’ll give it a greenfield project and see how it handles that.

item.title: Link Blog 3
item.description:
• I can waste hours looking at things like this Interactive World History Atlas since 3000 BC.
  • The BBC’s In Our Time is one of the best podcasts available. Although with around 30 years of old episodes it can be hard to find the one you are interested in (especially through RSS). Fear not, the Explore the In Our Time archive has you covered.
  • Why Is Venus Hell and Earth an Eden?. As the title suggests.
  • Learn X in Y minutes is a handy reminder tool for the syntax and basic control of most languages. I’ve already found it useful when needing to code in a long forgotten (by me) language.
  • Send this article to your friend who still thinks the cloud is a good idea. Interesting calculation of cloud vs hosted costs of an online service. I’ve always done the later.
  • BALL x PIT: My game of the year 2025 is a mildly interesting article about what the writer thinks BALL x PIT does right. I haven’t played the game, so can’t comment on that. What I found super interesting was a small point made near the end - the “Easy, Hard, Easy” loops in popular games on Steam. Damn, when I read that, it was a revelation. I have felt it as a player but not conceptualised it as a developer. Definitely something I will look to include in my games.
  • Internet security and avoiding ads (know that the two are intrinsically linked!) is important. How I block all online ads & An easy-to-use digital safety checklist are good lists of things that can be done to help. I haven’t done all the things listed, but certainly have gone through more than the basics.
